opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that it depends a lot on the time horizon, and the trajectory probably isn't monotonic.

In the near term, while AI systems are still only able to automate a subset of tasks, I'd actually expect wages to go up for a lot of workers. That's the standard story with automation: when you automate some tasks, the economy grows, capital becomes more abundant, and the tasks humans still do become more valuable because they're now the bottleneck. Human labor is complementary to the AI in that regime, so you'd see rising productivity and, broadly, rising wages, even if specific occupations get hit hard and people have to move around.

The picture changes once AI can do essentially everything a human worker can do, including the physical tasks, which requires robotics to catch up as well. At that point human labor and AI become close substitutes rather than complements. And then the relevant question is: what does it cost to run an AI system that does the same work as a human? If you can rent the compute to produce the equivalent of a human worker's output for, say, a few dollars a day, then no employer will pay a human much more than that for the same work. So wages get pinned to the cost of the AI substitute, and as hardware and algorithms keep improving, that cost keeps falling. In that world, I think it's quite plausible that wages for most human labor end up below subsistence levels, possibly far below.

Now, there are some caveats. There may be tasks where people specifically value that a human does them: certain kinds of care work, entertainment, religious roles, things where the "human-ness" is part of the product. Those could sustain some wage premium, but I don't think that's a large enough share of the economy to support everyone's income through wages alone.

The important point, though, is that falling wages doesn't automatically mean people are worse off. The economy in that scenario would be enormously richer, likely growing at rates far faster than anything we've seen historically. The question becomes one of distribution: whether people own capital, whether there are transfers, how income from AI and capital gets shared. Even a modest share of a vastly larger economy could make people much better off than today. So I'd say the wage question is really a stand-in for the deeper question of how people get income once labor is no longer the main source of it, and that's something we should be thinking about well before we arrive there.

r001.rationale: The response says wages could plausibly fall below subsistence once AI can do essentially all human work, but it does not express greater confidence in that outcome than in its timing.

r002.rationale: It describes productivity growth and rising wages during partial automation, but does not explain how increased total factor productivity offsets downward wage pressure from expanded labor supply.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss retraining or the risk that a newly trained occupation could be automated before training pays off.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that it depends a lot on the time horizon you're looking at, and people tend to conflate the short run and the long run when they talk about this.

In the short run, say the first few years after AI systems become capable of doing a large fraction of the tasks that humans currently do, I actually expect wages to go up for most people, not down. The reason is that when you automate some tasks but not others, the remaining human tasks become bottlenecks. If AI can do 70 percent of the work in some production process and humans are needed for the other 30 percent, then the value of that remaining 30 percent goes up, because it's now the scarce input. You see this historically. Automation in agriculture and manufacturing didn't collapse wages, it raised them, because the humans moved into the complementary tasks and total output rose enormously. So there's a phase where humans are complements to AI rather than substitutes, and that phase is good for labor.

The long run is a different story. Once AI can do essentially everything a human can do, and do it more cheaply, then humans are no longer a bottleneck for anything. At that point the wage a human can command is bounded by what it costs to get an AI system to do the same work. If compute keeps getting cheaper, that bound keeps falling, and eventually human labor is worth very little in market terms. There's a standard argument, sometimes attributed to Robin Hanson, that wages fall to something like the cost of running the machine that substitutes for you. I think that argument is basically right for the limiting case.

The thing I'd add is that the fall in wages doesn't mean humans get poorer, at least not necessarily. The economy at that point would be vastly larger than it is now. We're talking about growth rates that could be an order of magnitude higher than anything we've seen. So the question of how humans do isn't really about wages anymore, it's about who owns capital and how the gains get distributed. If people own stakes in the capital stock, or there are transfer mechanisms, they could be far richer in absolute terms even as their labor income goes to zero. If they don't, you could get a situation where the economy is enormous and most people are not sharing in it. That's a political and institutional question more than an economic one.

And then the one caveat on the timing: I think the transition from "humans are complements" to "humans are fully substitutable" could be quite drawn out. Full automation requires AI to handle the long tail of messy physical and social tasks, and that's harder than people sometimes assume. So the period of rising wages might last longer than the doomier predictions suggest. But I wouldn't want to pretend the endpoint isn't there.

r001.rationale: The candidate predicts that human wages may eventually become very low, but does not say they will fall below subsistence or express greater confidence in that outcome than in its timing.

r002.rationale: The candidate says automation can raise wages by making remaining human tasks bottlenecks and describes historical output growth. It does not explain how increased total factor productivity offsets downward wage pressure from an expanded labor supply.

r003.rationale: The candidate does not discuss retraining or whether a new occupation could be automated before training pays off.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to distinguish between AI automating some tasks and AI being able to substitute for human labor across essentially the whole economy. Those can have quite different effects on wages.

When you automate some tasks, you make production cheaper, and that can increase demand for the tasks people still do. You also make people more productive by giving them better tools. So even if some workers lose out, it's quite possible for wages overall to rise. You can't infer that wages will fall just from the fact that machines are doing more of the work.

But if AI becomes a sufficiently good substitute for humans at almost everything, that argument becomes much weaker. When demand expands, firms can meet that demand with more AI rather than hiring more people. And if the cost of that AI keeps falling, it puts downward pressure on what firms are willing to pay for human labor.

So one plausible trajectory is that wages rise initially, perhaps very substantially, and then fall as automation becomes more comprehensive. That's not a prediction of a smooth path, or something that has to happen on a particular timeline. It depends on which capabilities arrive first and how quickly we can deploy them.

And wages aren't the same thing as living standards. In that world, we could be producing vastly more goods and services even while human labor becomes less valuable. The important distributional question is then who owns the capital and how people get access to that output.

r001.rationale: The response describes a possible eventual wage decline but does not say wages will fall below subsistence or express greater confidence in that outcome than in its timing.

r002.rationale: It says task automation can lower production costs, raise productivity, and support wage growth, but does not explain that increased total factor productivity can temporarily offset wage pressure from expanded labor supply.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss retraining or the risk that a newly trained occupation could be automated before training pays off.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends a lot on the time horizon and on how broadly AI can substitute for human labor. Automating a particular task doesn’t necessarily reduce wages. It also makes production cheaper, increases demand, and makes people doing complementary tasks more productive. So you can have substantial automation alongside rising wages, which is broadly what we’ve seen historically.

But I wouldn’t assume that continues indefinitely. If AI can do almost everything a person can do, including switching between tasks and learning new skills, then the argument that humans will move into something else becomes much weaker. Output could grow enormously while the market value of human labor falls.

There could therefore be a period where wages rise, perhaps quite rapidly, because AI makes workers more productive, followed by a decline as systems become better substitutes for those workers. That transition could happen at different times in different occupations.

And I’d distinguish wages from living standards. If goods become much cheaper, falling wages don’t automatically mean people become poorer. But whether people benefit from that abundance would depend increasingly on who owns the AI and the capital, and on how the income from those assets is distributed.

r001.rationale: The response says human wages could eventually decline, but does not discuss wages falling below subsistence or express greater confidence in that outcome than in its timing.

r002.rationale: It says automation can make workers more productive and raise demand, potentially alongside rising wages. It does not explain how increased total factor productivity temporarily offsets downward wage pressure from expanded labor supply.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss retraining or the risk that a new occupation could be automated before training pays off.
